balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue mix
segmentRevenue.content:
Rockwell reports three operating segments: Intelligent Devices (drives, motion, sensing), Software & Control (PlantPAx, FactoryTalk, Logix, plus the higher-margin software/subscription mix), and Lifecycle Services (consulting, systems integration, managed services).

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: Intelligent Devices is the largest and most cyclical segment (hardware tied to capex and the FY2021-24 boom-bust); Software & Control carries the richest margin and is the growth story management points to on recurring/ARR metrics; Lifecycle Services is the smallest and most resilient.

What to watch:

  • Software & Control's share of total revenue trending up (mix shift supports the margin guide)
  • Intelligent Devices growth as the lead indicator of the capex cycle turning

segmentMargin.title: Segment operating margin
segmentMargin.content:
Each segment's operating income divided by its own revenue -- the profitability of the mix, not just its size.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: Corporate & Other (unallocated costs, a net drag) is excluded here since it has no revenue base to divide into; it is why segment margins sum to more than the enterprise margin shown elsewhere on this page.

What to watch:

  • Software & Control's margin versus Intelligent Devices' -- the gap is the case for the mix shift
  • Any segment's margin compressing while revenue grows (cost absorption, not just volume)

geoRevenue.title: Revenue by region
geoRevenue.content:
Revenue split across North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific and Latin America. Only disclosed annually in the 10-K, so this chart is FY-only.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: North America is roughly 60% of sales and carries most of the US industrial capex cycle's swings; China's weakness inside Asia Pacific has been a recurring management talking point through the FY2023-24 destock.

What to watch:

  • Asia Pacific/China growth as a read on manufacturing capex outside the US
  • Any region decoupling from the others (tariff or FX effects, not demand)

adjustedEBIT.title: Adjusted EBIT and margin
adjustedEBIT.content:
Adjusted EBIT strips the items management excludes from its guided metric -- restructuring, acquisition-related charges, asbestos-related costs and similar one-offs -- and is the basis for the Adjusted EBIT margin and Adjusted EPS the company guides to each quarter, not the GAAP operating income shown in the Growth & Profitability section above.

For Rockwell Automation, Inc.: FY2026 included asbestos-related charges and an IEEPA tariff-refund benefit that both hit GAAP but not (or only partly) this adjusted figure; FY2027 guidance is ~23% enterprise operating margin, up from FY2025's ~21.5%.

What to watch:

  • The gap between Adjusted EBIT margin and GAAP operating margin widening (more add-backs, lower quality)
  • Whether margin expansion is price/mix (durable) or cost timing (one quarter)
